top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B002) is the most defensible award on achievement, maturity, attribution and citation scope. The 1997 paper is a two-author origin of a distinct mechanism: collateral-linked borrowing limits feed back on asset prices and credit, turning temporary shocks into persistent, amplified ones. It has nearly three decades of theoretical, quantitative and policy use. No round-2 participant disputed its originality or its credit, and the narrow two-name citation leaves out nobody from the founding paper. My main reservation is empirical. The quantitative size of collateral amplification is less well identified than the theory's influence, and I treat the 2022 prize overlap as thematic rather than duplicative. P002 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, B012) is a serious second choice because the BLP framework has stayed standard through decades of critique. I rank it below P001 because the credit set is wider (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are omitted) and it relies on structural assumptions. I rank no award last because both substantive proposals describe mature, well-attributed achievements.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No credited name on P001 or P002 appears among my listed co-authors or networks. My main co-author, Magnus Johannesson, is a former committee member but not a candidate.
